genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman running the works grew up beside a wetland
her father taught her to turn the peat
she had noticed the decline of the birds nesting there
she trained at university in ecology
her first team replanted bare riverbanks
the young trees set too deep in the ground died
she then chose species able to stand standing water
passing birds came back once the reed cover closed over
she passes her method on to crews arriving from elsewhere
she holds that a damaged place mends through patience and not through machine power
text: The woman who now runs the restoration works grew up on the edge of a marsh. Her father taught her to turn the peat while she was still small, and she watched the brackish water rise and fall each year. By the time she left school she had noticed how few birds still nested there. She read ecology at university, then joined a team replanting bare riverbanks. That first attempt went badly: the saplings were set too deep and rotted in the waterlogged ground. She changed tack, picking species that could stand having their roots submerged, and spacing the holes more widely. Seasons later the reedbed had closed over itself and the passing birds came back. She now trains crews who travel in from other regions, and tells them the same thing: a damaged place mends through patience and watching, never through the force of machinery.

units: the narrator finds the shared composting site worth attention
the site rules turn away thick woody stems
a shredding machine was therefore installed
waste broken into chips rots down twice as fast as before
more people now use the site
the noise of the machine disturbs the flats at the bottom of the building
the compost is not screened before it is handed out
users therefore take away woody pieces they cannot use
the quality of the product changes from one bin to the next
the writer holds that a screen would put most of the fault right
text: Honestly, the shared compost heap round the corner is worth a look, even if the running of it limps in places. Whole branches are not allowed in, so a shredder had to go in beside the bins, and that machine is what changed everything: waste chopped into chips rots down in one season rather than two. People turn up more readily now, and there is usually a small queue by the gate. The catch is the racket. The motor howls, and the flats on the ground floor keep their windows shut through it. Someone explained to me that the finished compost ought to be screened before it is handed out; without that step gardeners go home with woody lumps they cannot use. The step is missing, so the stuff varies wildly from one bin to the next. My verdict is short: fine idea, wobbly execution, and a screen would put most of it right.

units: the writer is staying at a water treatment site
the water arriving carries nitrogen compounds
the level climbs after rain falls on the neighbouring crops
the metal pipes are under chemical attack
putting them right is costly
a planted wetland was laid out upstream
the plants clean the water before it reaches the tanks
the pollutant load drops by about a third
the energy the site uses falls as well
the team mean to enlarge the filtering area
text: I am writing to you from the water treatment works where I am spending the week, and I think what goes on here will interest you. The water arriving in the top basin carries nitrogen compounds, and the readings climb as soon as rain washes across the crops in the fields next door. The operators worry, because the metal pipework is being eaten away and putting it right costs a great deal of money. What they have settled on here surprised me by how plain it is. A shallow pool planted with reeds was dug above the site, and the plants clean the water before it ever reaches the tanks. The load drops by about a third, and the electricity bill falls with it. The team already mean to widen the filtering pool towards the meadow. I will tell you the rest when I am back; keep an evening free for me.

units: the text sets a lack of water against too much water in a river
the nature of the ground settles the answer
ground rich in silt holds back the rising water then lets it go slowly
a slope without plant cover sheds the water at once
the specialists do not plainly name the worse of the two
rising water brings nourishing deposits for all the damage it does
a lack of water makes the surface hard and squeezes the roots
the specialists rule out hard structures and deep wells
they call for a landscape mixing water stores, plant barriers and soils that let water through
text: Which should we fear more, a river running dry or a river breaking its banks? The question keeps coming back, and the answer depends on the ground you put it to. Silty flat land takes in the flood like a sponge and gives the water back over weeks; a bare hillside throws it downstream in a single afternoon. Ask which wound heals better and the specialists hesitate. A flood tears things away, yet it also lays down fertile silt, while drought bakes the surface hard and closes it round the roots. So what is to be done? No walls and no deep boreholes, they answer, but a landscape able to do both things at once: ponds that hold, hedges that slow the flow, loose soil that drinks. Only then is the comparison worth making, for one is cured by a slow water table and the other by remembering where the run-off went.

units: a technical manager sets out the procedure to people in training
her second speaks after each explanation
plant remains are no longer put under a covering layer
breaking down deep below gives off a gas that warms the air
the sorting pulls metals aside by magnetic attraction
plastics are parted by a jet of air
glass goes through a moving screen
the dark liquids from the heaps have to be drawn off before they reach the groundwater
a covering that lets air through holds down the smells
protective kit and a ban on walking about alone are imposed
text: The engineer in charge of the site went through the procedure with the trainees, and her deputy filled in after each point. She began by reminding them that garden and kitchen waste is no longer buried, since fermenting deep down gives off a gas with a strong warming effect. He then described the sorting line: metals lifted off by magnet, plastics blown aside by an air jet, glass dropping through a shaking screen. She stressed that the dark liquid seeping under the windrows has to be pumped away before it reaches the water table. Her deputy mentioned smell control, handled by a cover sheet that breathes and by a fine spray. She closed on safety: helmet, heavy gloves, and no walking alone between the skips. The trainees asked what becomes of the rejects, and the team promised them a look at the furnace.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first settled groups opened modest cropped spaces at the edge of the woods
the plant cover took the ground back once a group had left
making metal called for enormous amounts of wood fuel
whole blocks of woodland were then taken away
the slopes left without trees began to slip under the rain
official texts required the cutting back of branches instead of full felling
the flows of earth pushed those in charge to replant the slopes
these plantings often rested on a single species
that sameness left the woods open to insects
a mixture of species is now held to be the best protection
text: The earliest settled communities cleared only the fringes of the woods, opening glades wide enough for a crop and no wider. When a hamlet moved on, the canopy grew back over the ground it had used, so the forest outlived that first taking. Everything altered once metal was smelted in quantity, for the furnaces swallowed charcoal, and whole blocks of woodland went down together. Stripped hillsides then began to slip under heavy rain. Written rules followed, ordering that branches be cut back and the stools left standing rather than the trunk taken. Later, alarm at the sliding earth pushed those in authority to replant the slopes, very often with one species alone, and such even stands proved easy prey for insects. The lesson drawn since holds in a word: mixture, for a varied hillside withstands both pests and dry spells.

units: part of the carbon dioxide in the air passes into the seas
this dissolving alters the chemical make-up of the water
the sea surface turns more acid
living things with a chalky shell are struck first
their thinnest edges are eaten into and break down
these small organisms feed fish and seabirds
the weakening carries through to the whole food web
warmed water holds less dissolved gas
a share of the carbon therefore goes back to the air
shallow coastal stretches react before the rest, owing to farming inputs and water loaded with sediment
text: As the air takes on more carbon dioxide, the sea soaks up a large share of it, and that changes the chemistry of the water. The dissolved gas forms a weak acid, so the surface layer turns steadily sharper. Creatures that build a chalky shell feel it first: the shell forms poorly, and its thinnest edges start to pit and wear away. Since those tiny animals feed fish and seabirds alike, a weakness at the bottom works its way up through the whole food web. A second effect piles on. Warmer water holds less dissolved gas, so part of the carbon already taken up leaks back into the air, and the process keeps itself going. Readings taken near the coast show that shallow stretches react soonest, because they also receive muddy run-off and the fertiliser washed off the fields behind them.

units: the shared garden was very nearly left to go to waste
water stood between the rows from the first heavy rain
the young shoots rotted before they came to anything
turning the soil over more deeply changed nothing
the layer of clay brought the water back up
an experienced gardener worked out the real cause
the run-off was coming from the sloping car park
a planted ditch was cut along the edge of the ground
trees that drink water were put in and the beds were raised
the following season brought a heavy crop
text: We nearly gave up on the neighbourhood plot, and I can tell you the disappointment stung. The first real downpour left water standing between the rows, turning the ground into a bog where every seedling rotted where it stood. Someone suggested digging deeper. That achieved nothing, since the clay underneath simply pushed the water back up. A retired gardener finally explained that the trouble started elsewhere: the sloping car park was tipping its run-off straight onto us. So we cut a planted ditch along the fence, put in willows to drink the surplus, and raised the beds with salvaged timber. The following season the squashes covered half the ground and the lettuces held at last. We laugh about it now, about the boots that stuck fast and the drowned rows we mourned that summer.

units: the text sets two ways of dealing with kitchen scraps at home against each other
the room available steers the choice
the first answer uses a container that lets air through
wet matter and dry matter are laid down in turn
the mixture has to be stirred once a week
the finished product shows up after two seasons
the second answer means covering the scraps in a cut trench
the depth of cover keeps small animals away
the second answer costs nothing but yields nothing you can take back
the reader is asked to weigh up the space and the number of meals cooked
text: Anyone wanting to deal with peelings at home, rather than putting them out for collection, has two routes open to them, and the choice turns above all on how much room there is. The first means building an airy bin: you lay down a wet layer, then a dry one, stir the heap once a week, and lift out the dark crumbly stuff at the end of two seasons. The second is simply to bury the scraps in a trench and cover them over with a good depth of soil, enough to put rodents off. Set the two side by side: the bin asks for steady attention but hands you a feed ready to spread; the trench costs nothing at all and enriches the ground where it lies, though you will never lift a spadeful back out of it. To decide, measure your balcony or your plot, then count up how many meals get cooked at home each week.

units: the coast described is falling back under the waves
the posts put in recently are already leaning
the water drawn from the wells has taken on a salty taste
salt water is pushing on under the cropped land
the growers have given up the most delicate crops
they are turning to hardier plants that ask for less water
the cellars suffer from damp and salt breaks down their walls
the yard of the school was raised after a flood
the residents argue over holding the shoreline or moving the houses to higher ground
no decision has been taken locally
text: At first light the wind drops on the sea wall, and you can hear at last what this place is going through. Here, the water gains: every storm carries off a slice of the dune, and the posts driven in last year already lean inland. There, the wells: what comes up tastes of salt, a sign that the wedge of seawater is creeping under the gardens. Further on, the fields: growers have given up the tender crops and fallen back on tough varieties that ask for less water. Behind the bank, the cellars: damp climbs the walls and salt crumbles the bottom courses. At the end of the lane, the school yard, built up higher after the last flooding. And everywhere the same low conversation: hold the shoreline, or move the houses up to the ridge? Nobody here decides, but nobody pretends any more that the question is not there.
